'''Moses Ilyich Schönfinkel''' ({{langx|ru|Моисей Эльевич Шейнфинкель|translit=Moisei El'evich Sheinfinkel}}; 29 September 1888 – {{Death date text|1942}}) was a [[logician]] and [[mathematician]], known for the invention of [[combinatory logic]].

==Life==
Moses Schönfinkel was born on {{Birth date|1888|09|29|df=yes}} in Ekaterinoslav, Russian Empire (now Dnipro, Ukraine){{sfn|Wolfram|2020}} to a [[Jewish]] family. His father was Ilya Girshevich Schönfinkel, a merchant of first guild, who was in the grocery trade; his mother, Maria “Masha” Gertsovna Schönfinkel (née Lurie), came from the prominent [[Lurie]] family. Moses had siblings named Deborah, Natan, Israel and Grigoriy.{{sfn|Wolfram|2021a}} Schönfinkel attended [[Novorossiysk University]] of [[Odessa]], studying [[mathematics]] under [[Samuil Osipovich Shatunovskii]] (1859–1929), who worked in [[geometry]] and the [[foundations of mathematics]]. From 1914 to 1924, Schönfinkel was a member of [[David Hilbert]]'s group at the [[University of Göttingen]] in [[Germany]].{{sfn|Cardone|Hindley|2006}} On 7 December 1920 he delivered a talk entitled ''Elemente der Logik'' ("Elements of Logic") to the group where he outlined the concept of [[combinatory logic]]. [[Heinrich Behmann]], a member of Hilbert's group, later revised the text and published it in 1924.{{sfn|Curry|1927}} In 1928, Schönfinkel had one other paper published, on special cases of the decision problem (''[[Entscheidungsproblem]]''), which was prepared by [[Paul Bernays]].{{sfn|Kline|Anovskaa|1951}}

After he left Göttingen, Schönfinkel returned to Moscow. By 1927 he was reported to be mentally ill and in a sanatorium.{{sfn|Curry|1927}}{{sfn|Kline|Anovskaa|1951}} His later life was spent in poverty, and he died in Moscow some time in {{Death year and age|1942|1888}}. His papers were burned by his neighbors for heating.{{sfn|Kline|Anovskaa|1951}}

==Work==
Schönfinkel developed a formal system that avoided the use of [[bound variables]]. His system was essentially equivalent to a combinatory logic based upon the combinators '''B''', '''C''', '''I''', '''K''', '''S''' and a combinator for a universally quantified '''nand''' function which he called '''U'''. Schönfinkel stated that the system could be reduced to just '''K''', '''S''', and '''U''' (a colleague stated that '''U''' could be factored to the end of any expression and thus not always explicitly written) and outlined a proof that a version of this system had the same power as [[predicate logic]].{{sfn|Curry|1927}}

His paper also showed that functions of two or more arguments could be replaced by functions taking a single argument.{{sfn|Strachey|2000|loc=There is a device originated by Schönfinkel, for reducing operators with several operands to the successive application of single operand operators.}}{{sfn|Reynolds|1998|loc=In the last line we have used a trick called Currying (after the logician H. Curry) to solve the problem of introducing a binary operation into a language where all functions must accept a single argument. (The referee comments that although "Currying" is tastier, "Schönfinkeling" might be more accurate.)}}{{sfn|Slonneger|Kurtz|1995|p=144}} This replacement mechanism simplifies work in both combinatory logic and [[lambda calculus]] and would later be called [[currying]], after [[Haskell Curry]]. While Curry attributed the concept to Schönfinkel, it had already been used by [[Gottlob Frege|Frege]]{{refn|[[Willard Van Orman Quine]]: Introduction to "Bausteine der mathematischen Logik" ({{harvtxt|Schönfinkel|1967}})}} (an example of [[Stigler's law of eponymy|Stigler's law]]).

The complete known published output of Schönfinkel consists of just two papers: his 1924 ''On the Building Blocks of Mathematical Logic'', and another, 31-page paper written in 1927 and published 1928, coauthored with Paul Bernays, entitled ''Zum Entscheidungsproblem der mathematischen Logik'' (''On the Decision Problem of Mathematical Logic'').
